CHAPTER IV

It was near four o'clock in the afternoon. Eli was in the shop. His
eldest and youngest sons were abroad. Catherine and her little crippled
daughter had long been anxious about Gerard, and now they were gone a
little way down the road, to see if by good luck he might be visible
in the distance; and Giles was alone in the sitting-room, which I will
sketch, furniture and dwarf included.

The Hollanders were always an original and leading people. They claim
to have invented printing (wooden type), oil-painting, liberty,
banking, gardening, etc. Above all, years before my tale, they invented
cleanliness. So, while the English gentry, in velvet jerkins and
chicken-toed shoes, trode floors of stale rushes, foul receptacle of
bones, decomposing morsels, spittle, dogs, eggs, and all abominations,
this hosier's sitting-room at Tergou was floored with Dutch tiles, so
highly glazed and constantly washed, that you could eat off them. There
was one large window; the cross stone-work in the centre of it was
very massive, and stood in relief, looking like an actual cross to the
inmates, and was eyed as such in their devotions. The panes were very
small and lozenge-shaped, and soldered to one another with strips of
lead: the like you may see to this day in our rural cottages. The chairs
were rude and primitive, all but the arm-chair, whose back, at right
angles with its seat, was so high that the sitter's head stopped two
feet short of the top. This chair was of oak, and carved at the summit.
There was a copper pail, that went in at the waist, holding holy water,
and a little hand-besom to sprinkle it far and wide; and a long, narrow,
but massive oak table, and a dwarf sticking to its rim by his teeth, his
eyes glaring, and his claws in the air like a pouncing vampire. Nature,
it would seem, did not make Giles a dwarf out of malice prepense; she
constructed a head and torso with her usual care; but just then her
attention was distracted, and she left the rest to chance; the result
was a human wedge, an inverted cone. He might justly have taken her to
task in the terms of Horace,

     “Amphora coepit
     Institui; currente rota cur urceus exit?”

His centre was anything but his centre of gravity. Bisected, upper Giles
would have outweighed three lower Giles. But this very disproportion
enabled him to do feats that would have baffled Milo. His brawny arms
had no weight to draw after them; so he could go up a vertical pole like
a squirrel, and hang for hours from a bough by one hand like a cherry by
its stalk. If he could have made a vacuum with his hands, as the lizard
is said to do with its feet, he would have gone along a ceiling. Now,
this pocket-athlete was insanely fond of gripping the dinner-table with
both hands, and so swinging; and then--climax of delight! he would seize
it with his teeth, and, taking off his hands, hold on like grim death by
his huge ivories.

But all our joys, however elevating, suffer interruption. Little Kate
caught Sampsonet in this posture, and stood aghast. She was her mother's
daughter, and her heart was with the furniture, not with the 12mo
gymnast.

“Oh, Giles! how can you? Mother is at hand. It dents the table.”

“Go and tell her, little tale-bearer,” snarled Giles. “You are the one
for making mischief.”

“Am I?” inquired Kate calmly; “that is news to me.”

“The biggest in Tergou,” growled Giles, fastening on again.

“Oh, indeed!” said Kate drily.

This piece of unwonted satire launched, and Giles not visibly blasted,
she sat down quietly and cried.

Her mother came in almost at that moment, and Giles hurled himself under
the table, and there glared.

“What is to do now?” said the dame sharply. Then turning her experienced
eyes from Kate to Giles, and observing the position he had taken up, and
a sheepish expression, she hinted at cuffing of ears.

“Nay, mother,” said the girl; “it was but a foolish word Giles spoke.
I had not noticed it at another time; but I was tired and in care for
Gerard, you know.”

“Let no one be in care for me,” said a faint voice at the door, and in
tottered Gerard, pale, dusty, and worn out; and amidst uplifted hands
and cries of delight, curiosity, and anxiety mingled, dropped exhausted
into the nearest chair.

Beating Rotterdam, like a covert, for Margaret, and the long journey
afterwards, had fairly knocked Gerard up. But elastic youth soon
revived, and behold him the centre of an eager circle. First of all they
must hear about the prizes. Then Gerard told them he had been admitted
to see the competitors' works, all laid out in an enormous hall before
the judges pronounced.

“Oh, mother! oh, Kate! when I saw the goldsmiths' work, I had liked to
have fallen on the floor. I thought not all the goldsmiths on earth had
so much gold, silver, jewels, and craft of design and facture. But, in
sooth, all the arts are divine.”

Then, to please the females, he described to them the reliquaries,
feretories, calices, crosiers, crosses, pyxes, monstrances, and other
wonders ecclesiastical, and the goblets, hanaps, watches, Clocks,
chains, brooches, &c., so that their mouths watered.

“But, Kate, when I came to the illuminated work from Ghent and Bruges,
my heart sank. Mine was dirt by the side of it. For the first minute I
could almost have cried; but I prayed for a better spirit, and presently
I was able to enjoy them, and thank God for those lovely works, and
for those skilful, patient craftsmen, whom I own my masters. Well, the
coloured work was so beautiful I forgot all about the black and white.
But next day, when all the other prizes had been given, they came to the
writing, and whose name think you was called first?”

“Yours,” said Kate.

The others laughed her to scorn.

“You may well laugh,” said Gerard, “but for all that, Gerard Eliassoen
of Tergou was the name the herald shouted. I stood stupid; they thrust
me forward. Everything swam before my eyes. I found myself kneeling on
a cushion at the feet of the Duke. He said something to me, but I was so
fluttered I could not answer him. So then he put his hand to his side,
and did not draw a glaive and cut off my dull head, but gave me a gold
medal, and there it is.” There was a yell and almost a scramble. “And
then he gave me fifteen great bright golden angels. I had seen one
before, but I never handled one. Here they are.”

“Oh, Gerard! oh, Gerard!”

“There is one for you, our eldest; and one for you, Sybrandt, and for
you, Little Mischief; and two for thee, Little Lily, because God hath
afflicted thee; and one for myself, to buy colours and vellum; and nine
for her that nursed us all, and risked the two crowns upon poor Gerard's
hand.”

The gold drew out their characters. Cornelis and Sybrandt clutched each
his coin with one glare of greediness and another glare of envy at Kate,
who had got two pieces. Giles seized his and rolled it along the floor
and gambolled after it. Kate put down her crutches and sat down, and
held out her little arms to Gerard with a heavenly gesture of love and
tenderness; and the mother, fairly benumbed at first by the shower of
gold that fell on her apron, now cried out, “Leave kissing him, Kate;
he is my son, not yours. Ah. Gerard! my boy! I have not loved you as you
deserved.”

Then Gerard threw himself on his knees beside her, and she flung her
arms round him and wept for joy and pride upon his neck.

“Good lad! good lad!” cried the hosier, with some emotion. “I must go
and tell the neighbours. Lend me the medal, Gerard; I'll show it my good
friend Peter Buyskens; he is ever regaling me with how his son Jorian
won the tin mug a shooting at the butts.”

“Ay, do, my man; and show Peter Buyskens one of the angels. Tell him
there are fourteen more where that came from. Mind you bring it me
back!”

“Stay a minute, father; there is better news behind,” said Gerard,
flushing with joy at the joy he caused.

“Better! better than this?”

Then Gerard told his interview with the Countess, and the house rang
with joy.

“Now, God bless the good lady, and bless the dame Van Eyck! A benefice?
our son! My cares are at an end. Eli, my good friend and master, now we
two can die happy whenever our time comes. This dear boy will take our
place, and none of these loved ones will want a home or a friend.”

From that hour Gerard was looked upon as the stay of the family. He
was a son apart, but in another sense. He was always in the right, and
nothing too good for him. Cornelis and Sybrandt became more and more
jealous of him, and longed for the day he should go to his benefice;
they would get rid of the favourite, and his reverence's purse would be
open to them. With these views he co-operated. The wound love had
given him throbbed duller and duller. His success and the affection and
admiration of his parents made him think more highly of himself, and
resent with more spirit Margaret's ingratitude and discourtesy. For all
that, she had power to cool him towards the rest of her sex, and now for
every reason he wished to be ordained priest as soon as he could pass
the intermediate orders. He knew the Vulgate already better than most of
the clergy, and studied the rubric and the dogmas of the Church with
his friends the monks; and, the first time the bishop came that way, he
applied to be admitted “exorcist,” the third step in holy orders. The
bishop questioned him, and ordained him at once. He had to kneel, and,
after a short prayer, the bishop delivered to him a little MS. full of
exorcisms, and said: “Take this, Gerard, and have power to lay hands
on the possessed, whether baptized or catechumens!” and he took it
reverently, and went home invested by the Church with power to cast out
demons.

Returning home from the church, he was met by little Kate on her
crutches.

“Oh, Gerard! who, think you, hath sent to our house seeking you?--the
burgomaster himself.”

“Ghysbrecht Van Swieten! What would he with me?”

“Nay, Gerard, I know not. But he seems urgent to see you. You are to go
to his house on the instant.”

“Well, he is the burgomaster: I will go; but it likes me not. Kate, I
have seen him cast such a look on me as no friend casts. No matter; such
looks forewarn the wise. To be sure, he knows.”

“Knows what, Gerard?”

“Nothing.”

“Nothing?”

“Kate, I'll go.”

It was nearing four in the afternoon. Eli sat in his shop, while his eldest and youngest sons were away from home. Catherine and her frail daughter had been anxious all day about Gerard, and now they’d walked a short way down the road, hoping against hope to catch sight of him returning. In the quiet sitting-room, only Giles remained—alone with the furniture, and with himself.

Let me describe this room, as it stood then: plain, but clean, and full of character. The Dutch people had long been known for their ingenuity and industry. They claimed to have invented printing (with wooden type), oil painting, banking, gardening, and even liberty. But above all, years before this tale began, they had perfected cleanliness. While English nobles trod through floors covered in stale rushes, littered with bones, spoiled food, spittle, dogs, eggs, and every sort of filth, this humble hosier’s house in Tergou had floors of polished Dutch tiles—so bright and often washed that one could eat off them without fear.

There was one large window, its central stone crosswork thick and bold, rising like a true cross in the eyes of those who looked upon it. It stood out in relief, and during prayers, the family would turn their gaze toward it as if it were a sacred symbol. The glass panes were small, shaped like diamonds, and joined together with strips of lead—a style still seen today in country cottages.

The chairs were rough and simple, save for one armchair, whose back rose straight up at a right angle to the seat, so tall that the head of anyone seated in it barely reached the top. It was carved from oak, with a design at its peak. Beside it stood a copper pail, shaped like a woman's waist, filled with holy water, and next to it a tiny hand broom used to sprinkle blessings across the room. A long, narrow oak table dominated the space—and perched on its edge, clinging by his teeth, was Giles, the dwarf.

Nature, it seemed, had not meant to make Giles small out of spite. She had formed his head and torso with care—but then, distracted, she left the rest to chance. The result was a human wedge, an inverted cone. His upper body was massive, his lower limbs thin and stunted. He might well have quoted Horace: *“Amphora coepit institui; currente rota cur urceus exit?”* —“A jar was begun to be made; why did a jug come out?” His center of gravity was far from his physical center. If cut in half, the upper part would outweigh three times the lower. Yet this very imbalance gave him astonishing strength. His arms, powerful and unburdened by weight, allowed him to climb vertical poles like a squirrel or hang from a tree branch by one hand, suspended like a cherry on its stem. Had he possessed the suction power of a lizard’s feet, he might have walked across ceilings.

And yet, this miniature athlete had a peculiar passion: gripping the dinner table with both hands and swinging from it. And when he reached the height of joy? He’d clamp his jaws around the edge, release his hands, and hang there, trembling with delight, held fast by his great white teeth.

But such pleasures rarely last. Little Kate caught him mid-swing, and froze in horror. She was her mother’s daughter—her heart lay with order and propriety, not with the antics of a twelve-month-old gymnast.

“Oh, Giles! How can you? Mother is coming!” she cried.

“Go tell her, little tattletale,” growled Giles, refusing to let go. “You’re the one who causes all the trouble.”

“Am I?” she asked calmly. “That’s news to me.”

“The biggest mischief-maker in Tergou,” he snarled, resuming his grip.

“Oh, indeed?” she replied dryly.

The remark landed like a dart. Giles didn’t flinch. Instead, Kate sat down quietly and began to cry.

At that moment, her mother entered. Giles dropped instantly beneath the table, glaring up from the shadows.

“What’s going on now?” the woman demanded sharply.

Her eyes swept from Kate to the hidden figure under the table. Seeing his position and the guilty look on his face, she raised a hand as if to strike.

“Nay, mother,” said Kate softly. “It was only a foolish word. I wouldn’t have minded at another time—but I was tired, and worried about Gerard, you know.”

“Let no one worry over me,” whispered a weak voice at the door.

Gerard stumbled in—pale, dusty, exhausted. Hands shot up in surprise and delight, mingling with concern and joy. He collapsed into the nearest chair, spent from his journey.

He had raced through Rotterdam like a hunted animal, fleeing after Margaret, then endured a long, grueling ride home. The effort had worn him down completely. But youth is resilient. Soon, he revived—and became the focus of everyone’s attention.

They clamored to hear about the prizes first. Then Gerard told them how he’d been allowed to view all the competitors’ works laid out in a vast hall before the judges delivered their verdicts.

“Oh, mother! Oh, Kate!” he exclaimed. “When I saw the goldsmiths’ pieces—I nearly fell to my knees. I thought all the goldsmiths in the world couldn’t have produced so much gold, silver, jewels, and artistry. Truly, all crafts are divine.”

To please the women, he described the reliquaries, feretories, chalices, croziers, crosses, pyxes, monstrances—the sacred treasures—and then the goblets, hanaps, watches, clocks, chains, brooches—each piece dazzling in its detail. Their mouths watered at the thought.

“But when I came to the illuminated manuscripts from Ghent and Bruges,” he continued, “my heart sank. Mine looked like dirt beside theirs. For a moment, I almost wept. But I prayed for a better spirit, and soon I could admire them—thank God for such beauty, and for the patient artisans who created them. I forgot all about black-and-white work.”

Then, the next day, when all other prizes had been awarded, they came to the writing competition.

“And whose name do you think was called first?” he asked.

“Yours,” Kate guessed.

The others laughed at her.

“You may laugh,” Gerard said, “but it was true. Gerard Eliassoen of Tergou—that was the name the herald shouted. I stood stunned. They pushed me forward. Everything swam before my eyes. I found myself kneeling on a cushion at the Duke’s feet. He spoke to me, but I was too flustered to reply. Then he placed his hand at his side—not to draw a sword and behead me, but to give me a gold medal. Here it is.”

A cry erupted—almost a scuffle.

“And then,” he added, “he gave me fifteen golden angels. I’d seen one before, but never held one. Here they are.”

“Oh, Gerard! Oh, Gerard!”

“One for you, our eldest son,” he said, handing out coins. “One for you, Sybrandt. One for you, Little Mischief. Two for you, Little Lily—because God has afflicted you. One for myself—to buy colors and vellum. And nine for her who nursed us all and risked two crowns on poor Gerard’s hand.”

The gold brought out their true natures. Cornelis and Sybrandt grabbed their coins, eyes gleaming with greed—and envy, especially toward Kate, who received two. Giles snatched his and rolled it across the floor, chasing it like a child. Kate set aside her crutches, sat down, and stretched her arms toward Gerard with a gesture of pure love.

The mother, overwhelmed at first by the shower of gold landing in her apron, finally cried out: “Stop kissing him, Kate—he’s my son, not yours. Ah, Gerard! My boy! I’ve not loved you as you deserved.”

Gerard knelt beside her. She embraced him tightly, weeping with joy and pride upon his neck.

“Good lad! Good lad!” the hosier said, emotion in his voice. “I must go tell the neighbors. Lend me the medal, Gerard—I’ll show it to my friend Peter Buyskens. He always boasts about how his son Jorian won a tin mug at the archery butts.”

“Ay, go,” said Gerard. “And show him one of the angels. Tell him there are fourteen more just like it. But mind—you bring it back!”

“Stay a minute, father,” Gerard said, flushing with joy. “There’s better news.”

“Better than this?” someone gasped.

Gerard smiled. Then he told them of his meeting with the Countess—and the house rang with jubilation.

“Now, God bless the good lady—and bless the dame Van Eyck! A benefice? Our son? My cares are ended. Eli, my dear friend and master—we can die happy whenever our time comes. This dear boy will carry on for us. None of these children shall want a home or a friend.”

From that moment, Gerard was seen as the pillar of the family. He was not merely a son—he was special. Always right, always worthy. Nothing was too good for him.

Cornelis and Sybrandt grew more jealous with each passing day. They longed for the day he would leave for his benefice—when the favorite would be gone, and the priest’s purse would be open to them. Secretly, Gerard encouraged their hopes.

The wound love had dealt him throbbed less and less. His success, the affection of his parents, and the admiration of the village lifted his spirit. He began to resent Margaret’s coldness more fiercely. Yet she still held power over him—enough to make him wary of all women. For that reason, he now desired ordination more than ever.

He already knew the Vulgate better than most priests, studied church rubrics and doctrine with monks, and when the bishop visited, he applied to be admitted as an exorcist—the third step in holy orders.

The bishop questioned him—and ordained him immediately.

Gerard knelt. After a brief prayer, the bishop handed him a small manuscript filled with exorcisms.

“Take this, Gerard,” he said, “and have power to lay hands on the possessed—whether baptized or catechumens.”

Gerard accepted it reverently, and returned home bearing the Church’s authority to cast out demons.

As he stepped from the church, he met little Kate on her crutches.

“Oh, Gerard!” she said. “Who do you think sent for you? The burgomaster himself!”

“Ghysbrecht Van Swieten!” Gerard frowned. “What does he want?”

“I don’t know,” she replied. “But he seems urgent. You’re to go to his house at once.”

“Well,” Gerard said, “he is the burgomaster—I’ll go. But I don’t like it. Kate, I’ve seen him look at me… not like a friend. No matter. Such looks warn the wise. To be sure—he knows.”

“Knows what, Gerard?”

“Nothing.”

“Nothing?”

“Kate, I’ll go.”
